LIVE STREAMING AVAILABLE HERE Meeting ID: 870 6549 8518 Passcode: 100889 (Link can also be found on the County Website under Events Calendar – Click on Events Website) Staff Report CASE NUMBER: V-07-26 ADDRESS: 5362 Warrior Trail, Whiteland, Parcel #: 41-05-23-041-023.000-033 PETITIONER: Sandhu Properties INC, By Chad Leinart REQUEST VARIANCE OF USE of the Johnson County Unified Development Ordinance to allow for a trucking parking and trucking facility business (not permitted in a GB zoned property). PROPERTY DESCRIPTION This variance request involves a 12.696-acre parcel zoned GB (General Business). The property is currently unimproved, though it contains an existing dwelling that is not being used for residential purposes. The land is currently being utilized for parking. Surrounding land uses include: South: Several semi-tractor oriented businesses. North: Semi Parking, Warehouse, and manufacturing uses, including a similar use approved in 2023 by the Board of Zoning Appeals. All affected parcels, with the exception of 5440 Warrior Trail, are located within the Town of Whiteland limits VARIANCE OF USE REQUEST If approved, this Variance of Use request would allow the property to be redeveloped as a commercial truck parking lot, with the potential to repurpose the existing structure for fleet operations. Proposed Site Plan & Operations Parking Capacity: The submitted site plan proposes parking for approximately 71 semi-trucks and semi-trailers. Structure Reuse: The existing structure is proposed to be converted into an office building. Technical Review Adjustments: The final number of parking spots may be reduced during the Technical Review Committee (TRC) review of the civil plans to ensure compliance with development standards, including parking lot setbacks, landscaping, and drainage requirements. Hours of Operation: According to the petitioner’s submitted Plan of Operation, the facility will operate 24 hours a day with security. REGULATORY REQUIREMENTS The development will be required to go through the Technical Review Committee process and must adhere to the following:  All commercial standards in the zoning ordinance.  Procurement of a State Design Release for commercial use of the existing building.  Full compliance with all requirements of the Stormwater Management Ordinance. STAFF NOTES AND RECOMMENDATION This property has been continuously used for truck parking without authorization from staff, despite repeated enforcement notices from the department. However, staff notes that this formal application indicates the property owners are now making an effort to correct past violations and establish a compliant parking facility. If approved, this process will ensure the development is better suited for the area in both appearance and operational use. The existing dwelling on the property has previously been used by the property owner and guests as a social gathering spot, which has presented ongoing issues for the Town of Whiteland. The house is currently unfit for occupation. This unauthorized use must cease immediately, regardless of the outcome of this variance request. The Town of Whiteland has provided an official response to this use request, which is attached to this staff report for review. The requested variance is consistent with and similar to the uses of adjoining properties. Staff recommends the following conditions for consideration: 1. Required Approvals: The development must obtain all required permits and approvals before any improvements are made to the property. 2. Cease Existing Operations: All current semi-truck parking on the property must be removed until proper permits have been issued and site improvements are completed. 3. Structure Occupancy: The existing structure cannot be occupied or used until proper commercial permits have been obtained. 4. Nuisance Mitigation: If the structure is not brought into commercial use within one (1) year of this approval, it must be demolished and removed from the property to deter improper use and prevent a public nuisance. 5. Town Interlocal Agreement: The development must include and adhere to all stipulations provided by the Town of Whiteland. STAFF VARIANCE OF USE FINDINGS OF FACT: STAFF ANALYSIS 1. The approval will not be injurious to the public health, safety, morals, and general welfare of the community. The proposed conversion of the property into a secure, 24-hour commercial semi-truck parking facility will not be injurious to the public health, safety, or general welfare, provided all staff conditions are met. The property will undergo a rigorous Technical Review Committee (TRC) process to ensure proper drainage, stormwater management, landscaping, and setbacks are implemented. Furthermore, requiring the unapproved, hazardous use of the existing residential structure to cease and mandating its removal if not developed within one year directly mitigates an existing public nuisance and improves community safety. 2. The use and value of the area adjacent to the property included in the variance will be affected in a substantially adverse manner. The proposed use is highly consistent with the established character of the immediate area. The property is bordered to the south and north by semi-tractor-oriented businesses. By bringing this site into compliance through formal development standards, the physical appearance and operational safety of the site will be significantly upgraded compared to its current unauthorized state, thereby protecting adjacent property values. 3. The need for the variance does arise from some condition peculiar to the property involved. The 12.696-acre parcel is currently zoned GB (General Business), which does not permit the transportation and logistics support uses that have become dominant in this immediate area. Due to the intense semi-tractor traffic and industrial warehouse operations directly bordering the site to the north and south, it is highly impractical for this property to be developed for any of the retail or light commercial uses standardly permitted in the GB district. The unique physical location of the parcel—effectively locked within a heavy industrial and transportation corridor—creates a distinct peculiarity where standard general business uses are no longer viable or compatible. 4. The strict application of the terms of the Zoning Ordinance will constitute an unnecessary hardship if applied to the property for which variance is sought. Strict adherence to the GB zoning text would restrict the property from fulfilling its most logical economic use as a support facility for the surrounding transport sector. Forcing standard retail or office development on a site locked between semi-truck facilities and manufacturing warehouses creates an unnecessary hardship, as such businesses would struggle with compatibility. Granting the variance allows the petitioner to formalize and legally rectify the land use in a way that matches the market reality of the corridor. 5. The approval does not interfere substantially with the Comprehensive Plan. The Comprehensive Plan’s recommendation for mixed use in this area. Mixed uses development is intended to encourage a well-planned, integrated mix of compatible uses that relate well and support one another. This use is compatible with other uses in the area. GENERAL INFORMATION Applicant: Chad Leinart 3200 Sycamore Ct, Ste 2A Columbus IN 47203 Owner: Sandhu Properties Inc 5362 Warrior Trl Whiteland IN 46143 Zoning: GB Land Use: undeveloped land, parking Future Land Use: Mixed -use ~MNH V-07-26 Base Map subject site V-07-26 Base Map II V-07-26 AERIAL Proposed Plan of Operation, V-07-26 V-07-26 Petitioner’s Findings of Facts 6/11/2026 Members of the Johnson County Board of Zoning Appeals Re: V-07-26 Sandhu Properties INC 5362 Warrior Trail The Town of Whiteland (TOW) has been made aware of the request for a use variance for the property located at 5362 Warrior Trail, which is located in Johnson County. • Warrior Trail, which is owned by the Town of Whiteland, is only designated for 11,000 lbs and is not designated for truck traffic from 790’ north of Whiteland Rd. to the end of Warrior Trail. The road that was put into place for the neighboring parcel at 5440 Warrior Trail was regulated to have no more than 35 trucks. The road has been installed less than 18 months, and that portion of the road is already failing. With an already failing road, adding additional trucks will only add to the problem that has been created by the previous trucking development. See attached photos that were taken on June 9, 2026. • Stormwater. This site, since 2020 has increased impervious surface with no regards to any type of improvements on drainage. • IDEM/County Drainage Board/Municipal permits. As they have seemingly changed the overall layout of the property, have they ever obtained any permits for the improvements that have been made on this parcel? Have they ever reached out to the local jurisdiction for any type of official improvement or inquired about what would be required of them? • The TOW police department has made numerous interactions on this property, and it has created a nuisance in the general area due to exterior condition of the property. This has been a blighted property within our community since the parcel owner has taken ownership. • The increase in truck traffic and the impact that this type of development would have on TOW owned infrastructure would not outweigh the positives that would come from this parcel. They would undoubtedly utilize the existing structure as an “office” but would but would continue to utilize in the same condition and occupancy it currently as a multi-family structure. The Town of Whiteland is concerned that allowing this type of development would ultimately lead to more issues and resources being utilized by our staff than the positives that would come from this type of development where there is already a litany of viable options with parcels to the south to allow for trucking facilities and truck parking. We kindly request that this variance be denied, due to the state statute requirements for being granted a use variance based on IC 36-7-4-918.4 which requires: 1. “The approval will not be injurious to the public health, safety, morals, and general welfare of the community” - This would disproportionally represent the injurious portion to the Town of Whiteland as we have had multiple police resources and code enforcement regarding trash and rubbish in the area. Adding to the additional issues we’ve already seen with the neighboring parcel, this would only add additional trucks and usage on the TOW infrastructure. 2. “the strict application of the terms of zoning ordinance will constitute an unnecessary hardship if applied to the property for which the variance is sought” - Purchasing a property with an intent that does not allow a permitted use of a zoned parcel does not constitute an “unnecessary hardship” rather a lack of planning on behalf of the parcel owner. Based off the Johnson County’s planning department definition within the current UDO states an “unnecessary hardship” Significant economic injury that: a. Arises from the strict application of zoning regulations in this ordinance to the conditions of a particular, existing parcel of property; b. Effectively deprives the parcel owner of all reasonable economic use of the parcel; and c. Is clearly more significant than compliance cost or practical difficulties. Furthermore, the existing structure doesn’t meet the setback requirements for GC zoning in the current UDO which requires front setbacks based off road designation (Collector/Local-40’, Minor Arterial-50’, I/Principal Arterial-60’). If the BZA does approve the use variance we would request the following commitments by the property owner: 1. Improve Warrior Trail with concrete from the Town limits to the end of Warrior Trail. The Town of Whiteland will be submitting for a Community Crossings Matching Grant program this Fall for reconstruction of Warrior Trail from Whiteland Rd to end of Town limits. This road will be converted to all concrete to ensure that it can withstand the truck traffic. 2. Apply for Town of Whiteland curb cut permit Sincerely, Carmen Young Billy Patrick Town Manager Building Commissioner Town of Whiteland Town of Whiteland Cc: Richard Hill, Whiteland Town Council President Derek Cox, Whiteland Town Marshal Warrior Trail (Photos taken 6.9.2026) Staff Report CASE NUMBER: V-8-26 ADDRESS: 2729 Hurricane Road, Franklin PETITIONER: Cara and Andrew Wagner REQUEST VARIANCE OF DEVELOPMENT STANDARDS of the Johnson County Unified Development Ordinance to provide for the construction of a 3,424 square foot accessory structure, where all accessory structures will total 4,844 square feet in building area, (The zoning ordinance allows aggregate accessory structure area to be no more than 100 % of the building area of the primary dwelling, or, in this case, 2,642 square feet). STAFF RECOMMENDATION: Staff recommends the approval of this variance request. PROPERTY DESCRIPTION This 2.82-acre site is zoned SR (Single-Family Residential) and is currently improved with a single-family dwelling and two accessory structures. The surrounding land uses include:  North & West: Parcels of a similar size, all utilized for residential purposes.  East: The Legends Golf Club.  South: A planned housing development located within the City of Franklin. The properties directly to the north, south, and east are located within the municipal limits of the City of Franklin. VARIANCE REQUEST – DEVELOPMENT STANDARD The applicant is requesting a Variance of Development Standard to allow the construction of a 3,424-square-foot accessory structure on the property. The site currently contains two accessory structures, an 850-square-foot structure used as a photography studio (previously approved via a Variance of Use) and a 570-square-foot detached garage. With the addition of the proposed 3,424-square-foot building, the total aggregate area of the three accessory structures would be 4,844 square feet. This exceeds the square footage of the primary dwelling, which is 2,642 square feet. The local zoning ordinance stipulates that the total aggregate area of all accessory structures cannot exceed 100% of the square footage of the primary dwelling. This structure will replace an old barn that was removed in 2025. The barn was 1,326 square feet in size. When evaluating variance requests for oversized accessory structures, the department typically considers three evaluation factors. Staff’s analysis of these factors for the subject property is detailed below: 1. Context & Density  Standard: The subject lot is located in a rural or agricultural area, or an area generally characterized by large lots and open, expansive spaces.  Analysis: While municipal expansion and nearby city development have increasingly surrounded this property, the site originally existed in a rural context and retains its large 2.82-acre footprint. The immediate area functions as a rural-residential pocket. Therefore, the property layout can comfortably absorb the physical footprint without creating a crowded or overly dense appearance. 2. Area Consistency  Standard: The subject lot is located in an area where oversized accessory structures are common.  Analysis: There are no other large accessory structures in the immediate area. However, because the subject tract is significantly larger than standard suburban lots (2.82 acres), it possesses the unique capacity to accommodate a larger structure without negatively impacting the neighborhood's pattern of development. 3. Visual Impact  Standard: The oversized accessory structure would be obscured from view from surrounding properties and public rights-of-way.  Analysis: The property is heavily landscaped with mature trees that effectively block the view of the structure from the public right-of-way and a majority of the neighboring residential properties. Conclusion Given that the structure will be well-screened from public view, sits on a substantial 2.82-acre lot, and aligns with the historical and regional presence of large outbuildings, staff asserts that the request represents an acceptable deviation from the zoning ordinance and recommends approval. VARIANCE OF DEVELOPMENT STANDARDS FINDINGS OF FACT: STAFF ANALYSIS 1. The approval will not be injurious to the public health, safety, morals, and general welfare of the community. Staff Analysis: The proposed 3,424-square-foot accessory structure will be utilized strictly for purposes accessory to a residential use and will replace an older 1,326-square-foot barn demolished in 2025. It will meet all required building codes and structural safety standards. Because the structure will be placed on a large 2.82-acre lot and used in a manner consistent with residential property management, its construction will pose no threat to the public health, safety, morals, or general welfare of the community. 2. The use and value of the area adjacent to the property included in the variance will not be affected in a substantially adverse manner. Staff Analysis: The placement of the proposed structure will be to the north, positioned directly behind an existing accessory building. The property is heavily screened by a dense growth of mature trees, which effectively obscures the structure from the public right-of-way and adjacent residential properties. While there are no other large accessory structures in the immediate neighborhood, the substantial size of the subject lot (2.82 acres) ensures that the oversized building will not crowd neighboring properties, diminish their use, or adversely affect adjacent property values. 3. The strict application of the terms of the Zoning Ordinance will result in practical difficulties in the use of the property. Staff Analysis: The primary residence on the subject property is an older home constructed without an attached garage. In modern home designs, an attached garage is included in the primary footprint, which inherently inflates the allowable aggregate square footage for future accessory buildings. Because this property relies on an existing 570-square-foot detached garage, that space is legally counted against the petitioner’s accessory structure allotment under the strict text of the ordinance. Restricting a large, 2.82-acre tract to standard suburban accessory limits under these specific architectural circumstances creates an unnecessary practical difficulty, punishing the owner for an older layout despite the property having ample physical space to absorb the new structure. 4. The variance is NOT primarily for the economic benefit of the petitioner. Staff Analysis: The requested variance is sought to allow the construction of a storage and personal-use outbuilding to replace a previously demolished barn. There is not economic benefit associated with this request. 5. The variance request IS the minimum deviation that is needed to be awarded to the applicant. Staff Analysis: . The applicant requires a structure of this size to adequately store property maintenance equipment and personal property necessary to manage a nearly 3-acre residential tract. The proposed square footage is proportional to the historical footprint of the property and its physical demands. It represents the minimum deviation necessary to allow the property owner a reasonable level of storage utility that matches the scale of their acreage. 6. The variance request is NOT due to a hardship caused by the current owners of the property. Staff Analysis: The proposed structure has not been constructed without approval, nor have materials been purchased in anticipation of approval. Because the petitioner is seeking formal authorization prior to initiating any development, there is no self-created hardship. GENERAL INFORMATION Applicant: Cara Wagner 2729 Hurricane Road Franklin, IN 46131 Owner: Same Zoning: SR (Single Family Residential) Land Use: Residential Future Land Use: Suburban Residential ~ MNH V-08-26 BASE MAP SUBJECT SITE V-08-26 AERIAL MAP V-08-26 AERIAL MAP II V-08-26 PETITIONER ‘S FINDING OF FACTS

JOHNSON COUNTY Department of Planning and Zoning (317) 346-4350 86 West Court Street www.JohnsonCounty.in.gov Franklin, Indiana 46131 Courthouse Annex MEETING AGENDA Johnson County Board of Zoning Appeals July 28th, 2026, 7:00 PM Public Auditorium, West Annex Building 86 West Court Street, Franklin, Indiana CALL TO ORDER ROLL CALL APPROVAL of MINUTES Meeting minutes from the June 23rd, 2026 meeting PUBLIC HEARINGS CONTINUED PETITIONS V-1-26. Darren Poynter, Vickie Poynter. 4912 Olive Branch Rd, Greenwood VARIANCE OF DEVELOPMENT STANDARDS of the Johnson County Uniﬁed Development Ordinance legally allows a 2,400-square-foot accessory structure, where all accessory structures will total 3,150 square feet in building area NEW PETITIONS V-9-26. BLF Acres LLC. 378 & 354 Western Blvd, and Lot 4 of Fairview West Commercial Subdivision. Greenwood VARIANCE OF USE of the Johnson County Uniﬁed Development Ordinance to allow for sales, repair, and rental of trailers, truck beds, and golf carts V-10-26. Richard Payne. 5998 Travis Road, Greenwood VARIANCE OF DEVELOPMENT STANDARDS of the Johnson County Uniﬁed Development Ordinance to provide for the construction of a 2,925 square foot accessory structure, where all accessory structures will total 4,461 square feet in building area. 1 In accordance with American Disabilities Act, any person attending the public meeting in need of reasonable accommodations in order to attend, hear, or present evidence at the public meeting on an agenda item should contact the Johnson County ADA coordinator, Barb Davis, at 86 W. Court St., Franklin, IN 46131, (317) 346-4329, bdavis@co.johnson.in.us. V-11-26. Putnam Properties LLC. 326 Western, Greenwood VARIANCE OF USE of the Johnson County Uniﬁed Development Ordinance to allow automobile and vehicle sales, repair, and rental services (not permitted in a Corridor Overlay District) V-12-26. Story Custom Development LLC. Approx. 3855 Olive Branch Road, Greenwood VARIANCE OF USE of the Johnson County Uniﬁed Development Ordinance to allow a group home use for senior living (not permitted in an SR, Single Family Residential District) V-13-26. Nineveh Township Volunteer Fire Dept. Approx. 8050 S. Nineveh Road, Nineveh. VARIANCE OF DEVELOPMENT STANDARDS of the Johnson County Uniﬁed Development Ordinance to allow for the following: 1. Chapter 3, Section B, 5, b: To omit the required 6-inch continuous concrete curb around the parking lot perimeter separating paved from non-paved surfaces. 2. Chapter 3, Section C, 5, c: To omit the required perimeter landscaping and buffering standards surrounding the parking lot. OLD BUSINESS None. NEW BUSINESS Status update V-7-26. Sandhu Properties Inc. 5362 Warrior Trail. Whiteland REPORTS AND RECOMMENDATIONS None. ADJOURNMENT The next regular meeting of the Johnson County Board of Zoning Appeals is scheduled for Tuesday, September 25th, 2026, at 7:00 PM. LIVE STREAMING AVAILABLE HERE Meeting ID: 870 6549 8518 Passcode: 100889 (Link can also be found on the County Website under Events Calendar – Click on Events Website) 2 Staff Report CASE NUMBER: V-1-26 ADDRESS: 4912 Olive Branch Road, Greenwood 46143 (parcel #: 41-09-32-014-001.000-034) PETITIONER: Darren Poynter, Vickie Poynter by David Gilman REQUEST VARIANCE OF DEVELOPMENT STANDARDS of the Johnson County Unified Development Ordinance legally allows a 2,400-square-foot accessory structure, where all accessory structures will total 3,150 square feet in building area. (The zoning ordinance allows aggregate accessory structure area to be no more than 100 % of the building area of the primary dwelling, or, in this case, 1,360 square feet). PROPERTY DESCRIPTION This 0.94-acre site is zoned SR (Single Family Residential) and improved with a residential home and two additional structures. The property is surrounded are similar-sized parcels used for residential on the north side of Olive Branch Road and larger lots used for residential on the south side of Olive Branch Road. Update for July Meeting The petition was continued at the April 28th 2025 meeting with the following motion: To continue V-1-26 to the July 27, 2026 meeting. The motion was based on staff recommendation since construction has not yet commenced and the violation remains on the property. As of July 21st 206, only some site preparation has occurred on the property. On 7/15/26, the property owner provided the following email from their subcontractor From: Cindy Fikes <cindy@mooreconstructionservices.net> To: Vickie Poynter <poynterv@sbcglobal.net> Sent: Tuesday, July 14, 2026 at 02:46:45 PM EDT Subject: Re: E-gress Info Hi Vickie, We are looking at 8/3 to get started on the foundation. I will let you know if we have any weather delays. Typically Daniel Cornett, the Stormwater specialist likes to come out before the digging starts. I will have Ian(Ken refers to him as Wes which is his middle name) reach out to Daniel a few days before we are getting started so he can meet him on site to discuss drainage, concrete clean out bags, etc. Once Brian our concrete guy gets started on the digging, we will coordinate the footer inspection which is when they come out to inspect the holes and make sure they are deep and wide enough before we pour concrete and start to install block. Thank you, Cindy Given the history of this case, the staff recommends that the Board grant a 60-day extension to ensure the property owner fulfills the requirements of the issued permit and shows evidence to resolve the existing violation. Update for April Meeting The petition was continued at the January 27, 2026, meeting with the following motion: 3 “To continue V-1-26 for ninety-one (91) days to allow the Petitioners to present compliant building plans and to remove spoils from the property.” Since the January meeting, the property owner has applied for and was issued a building permit in April for a primary residence addition. Once constructed, this addition will increase the square footage of the primary structure sufficiently to allow for the larger accessory structure currently under dispute. If the addition is completed, the requested variance will no longer be necessary. However, as construction on the addition has not yet commenced, the violation remains on the property. Given the history of this case, the staff recommends that the Board grant a 90-day extension to ensure the property owner fulfills the requirements of the issued permit and show evidence to resolves the existing violation. Regarding the second part of the motion, staff will provide an update at the meeting. VARIANCE REQUEST This variance request seeks approval to classify an existing 2,400-square-foot building as an accessory dwelling, despite it exceeding the maximum allowable square footage for accessory structures on a single tract of land. Under the current Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), the total area of all accessory structures is limited to the size of the primary residence. On this specific property, the primary dwelling measures 1,360 square feet. Because there is already an existing 750-square-foot detached garage, the addition of this 2,400- square-foot structure significantly exceeds the permitted allotment. The history of this structure began in June of 2023 when the property owners applied for a building permit for a primary dwelling addition following consultations with county staff. Due to the scale of the proposed project, the owners submitted plans depicting an attached addition rather than a detached building. The design featured a fully enclosed breezeway intended to connect the 2,400-square-foot structure to the main house. However, the connection was never built. As the permit neared expiration, staff notified the owners that failure to construct the breezeway resulted in a zoning violation, as the building remained a non-compliant detached structure. While several options exist to bring the property into compliance, the owners have chosen to seek a variance to bypass the requirement for the connecting breezeway. It is worth noting that when this project was initially permitted, the previous zoning ordinance was even more restrictive, limiting accessory structures to 50% of the primary dwelling's size and requiring that they not exceed the height of the main house. Both the previous and current standards are designed to ensure that accessory buildings remain secondary to the primary residence and preserve the character of single-family developments. Large, oversized accessory structures often fail to blend with neighborhood aesthetics and can inadvertently encourage land uses that are not typically permitted within residential districts. FINDINGS OF FACT: VARIANCE OF DEVELOPMENT STANDARDS 1. The approval will not be injurious to the public health, safety, morals, and general welfare of the community. The structure will not impact public health, safety, morals, or general welfare, as it will be verified that it is built to local and state building codes. 4 2. The use and value of the area adjacent to the property included in the variance will be affected in a substantially adverse manner. This oversizing is inconsistent with the established single-family character of the adjacent properties, there are no similar size structure in the area. A variance of similar requests could be sought by other property owners based on the same findings presented by the petitioner. 3. The strict application of the terms of the Zoning Ordinance will not result in practical difficulties in the use of the property. The petitioner has failed to demonstrate that there are unique physical circumstances or conditions particular to this specific parcel of land—such as irregular lot shape, exceptional topography, or pre- existing infrastructure—that prevent them from adhering to the established development standards for an accessory structure. The petitioner presented building and site plans that would achieve the standard set forth and attainable. The Petitioner’s findings of fact list the distance and elevation as problematic; the property owner decided to locate the structure in that spot. 4. The variance is not primarily for the economic benefit of the petitioner. While economic benefit is present with this variance and could be a secondary consequence, it is not the primary motive for the variance. 5. The variance request is not the minimum deviation that is needed to be awarded to the applicant. The applicant has failed to present compelling reasoning that the entire amount of the requested variance is essential to overcome the physical hardship. No data was presented demonstrating that a smaller, compliant, or near-compliant structure would not serve the basic intended purpose. Specific justification for the size has not been adequately documented or presented as a necessity that overrides the zoning standard. The request appears to be driven by desire rather than an absolute, physically necessary requirement. 6. The variance request is due to hardship caused by the current owners of the property. The petitioner had reasonable and feasible design options available that would have satisfied the ordinance requirements or substantially minimized the deviation sought. The pursuit of a non-conforming design, despite clear alternatives, means the hardship is one of choice or preference, not one inherent to the land itself. GENERAL INFORMATION Applicant: David Gilman 211 S Ritter Avenue, Ste H Indianapolis IN 46219 Owner: POYNTER DONALD L & POYNTER DARREN E & POYNTER VICKIE L 5035 Cordia CT Indianapolis, IN 46237 5 Current Zoning: SR (single-family residential ) Existing Land Use: Residential Future Land Use: Suburban Residential -MNH 6 Staff Report CASE NUMBER: V-09-26 ADDRESS: 378 & 354 Western Blvd, Greenwood & Lot 4 of the Fairview West Commercial Subdivision, Parcel #: 41-03-33-021-027.000-038 and 41-03-33-022-006.000-038 PETITIONER: BLF Acres LLC, By Bill Niemier REQUEST VARIANCE OF USE of the Johnson County Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) to allow for the sales, repair, and rental of trailers, truck beds, and golf carts within the Corridor Overlay District (COD), where such uses are prohibited. PROPERTY DESCRIPTION The subject property comprises two lots within the Fairview West Commercial Plat, located east of Interstate 69 (I-69) along Western Boulevard: Lot 3: 2.04 acres, currently improved with a vacant commercial building originally developed in 1997 as a fueling station and restaurant. Lot 4: 3.24 acres, currently undeveloped. These lots are not contiguous and are separated by Western Boulevard. Both lots are zoned GC (General Commercial) and fall within the Corridor Overlay District (COD). Surrounding properties consist of commercially developed lots of similar size and character. VARIANCE REQUEST The applicant proposes to operate a business focused on the sales, repair, and rental of trailers and golf carts, as well as the installation of truck beds. Under the UDO, this activity falls under Automobile/Vehicle Sales, Rental, Service, and Repair. This category is explicitly listed as a prohibited land use within the Corridor Overlay District (COD). Trailers would involve bumper-mounted flatbed, utility, car hauler, and enclosed trailers. It would not involve travel/recreational trailers or boat trailers. Historically, Western Boulevard connected directly to Fairview Road, a major commercial arterial adjacent to former State Road 37. During the conversion of SR 37 into I-69, the Indiana Department of Transportation (INDOT) permanently closed three intersections within unincorporated Johnson County, including the SR 37 and Fairview Road interchange. This closure altered local circulation patterns, reduced direct passerby traffic, and contributed to business relocations in the immediate area. In anticipation of I-69, Johnson County partnered with a planning consultant to develop the I-69 Corridor Plan, which was adopted in December 2018 as a supplement to the Johnson County Comprehensive Plan. The plan aimed to establish high-quality architectural and land-use standards for the I-69 gateway into the county, explicitly identifying certain vehicular-oriented commercial uses as undesirable for new development. When the county adopted the updated Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) in 2024, these plan recommendations were codified into the Corridor Overlay District (COD) regulations. The COD establishes elevated design and development standards for sites, structures, landscaping, signage, and site improvements within highly visible county corridors to: 7 Promote High-Quality Design: Encourage creative, innovative, and visually cohesive site and building development. Protect Property Values & Welfare: Preserve long-term property values and promote public health, safety, and welfare through consistent, coordinated development standards. Ensure Efficient & Coordinated Development: Establish high standards that optimize land use, permit flexible site design, and protect the functional integrity and visual character of major transportation corridors. Because the COD regulations explicitly prohibit automobile sales, service, and repair, the proposed operation requires Use Variance approval from the Board of Zoning Appeals. The Future Land Use Map within the I-69 Corridor Plan designates this immediate area for Residential development. However, staff believes this designation was an analytical oversight during the 2018 planning process, as this specific node south of Fairview Road contains existing, built-out commercial development that is not discussed or recommended for residential transition elsewhere in the document. Staff feels a Mixed-Use designation would have been more appropriate for this node. The overall narrative of the I-69 Corridor Plan explicitly seeks to maintain economic vitality and support the adaptive reuse of existing commercial properties impacted by INDOT access closures along secondary frontage networks. While general commercial reuse of this built-out site aligns with the plan's economic vitality goals, auto sales and repair specifically are restricted by the COD regulations to uphold the corridor’s elevated visual standards—hence the necessity of the requested Use Variance. While this report focuses primarily on the land use request, any future development of the vacant Lot 4 will be subject to the standard Site Plan Review process. Lot 4 must adhere to all UDO development standards. Staff notes that the preliminary layout shown on the submitted site plan will likely change once formal site development and drainage requirements are fully engineered. No Development Standard Variances are requested at this time, as the petitioner wishes to secure land use approval prior to committing to full site engineering. To address potential visual impacts on the corridor without requiring immediate development variances, Staff has drafted specific conditions of approval aimed at managing outdoor staging and display areas. STAFF RECOMMENDATION Should the Board move to approve this request, Staff recommends the inclusion of the following commitments/conditions: 1. Lot 4 Use Restriction: Lot 4 shall be utilized exclusively for product display and staging. 2. Surfacing Requirement: Any development or staging area on Lot 4 shall be constructed with a hard, durable surface. 3. The product display and staging area shall be subject to the same standards as a parking lot, especially Chapter 3 Section 3,c and Section B,5,b,c and Chapter 3 Section C,5,c. Staff would strongly suggest considering interior landscaping as well if the paved area is to be over 1.5 acres. 8 4. Fencing Standards: If fencing is installed on Lot 4, chain-link fencing (with or without barbed wire) is strictly prohibited. Fencing must consist of wrought iron or high-quality privacy fencing materials. 5. No Outdoor Storage of Repair/Parts: No outdoor storage of items awaiting repair, salvage parts, or loose materials shall be permitted on either parcel (Lot 3 or Lot 4). FINDINGS OF FACT: USE VARIANCE State Requirement: The approval will not be injurious to the public health, safety, morals, and general welfare of the community. The subject site includes an existing, vacant commercial building on Lot 3 originally developed in 1997. Granting a Use Variance to allow the sales, repair, and rental of trailers, truck beds, and golf carts within this existing structure returns a vacant property to productive commercial use. Furthermore, restricting Lot 4 strictly to a heavily conditioned, high-quality staging and display area (or leaving it undeveloped) prevents unmitigated commercial expansion, thereby safeguarding the visual environment, public safety, and general welfare of the corridor. State Requirement: The use and value of the area adjacent to the property included in the variance will not be affected in a substantially adverse manner. Reoccupying the vacant building on Lot 3 eliminates a long-standing vacancy that risks becoming a visual blight along Western Boulevard following INDOT's access closures. Surrounding properties are established commercial lots of similar character. By revitalizing the existing structure, the variance stabilizes local property values. To protect adjacent parcels from potential visual degradation associated with expanding commercial operations, approval is tied to strict conditions that prohibit open storage of parts or items needing repair and ensure that any use of the vacant Lot 4 is strictly limited to screened display rather than intensive site development or heavy industrial staging. State Requirement: The need for the variance arises from some condition peculiar to the property involved. The property features a unique duality: a fully built-out commercial structure (Lot 3) that was rendered vacant and functionally isolated due to INDOT's closure of the Fairview Road/SR 37 intersection, paired with an adjacent undeveloped parcel (Lot 4) separated by a public road. The existing building was constructed under prior standards for vehicular commercial activity, making its footprint well-suited for adaptive indoor reuse. However, the 2024 Corridor Overlay District (COD) standards strictly prohibit these land uses. This structural layout—a purpose-built commercial building stranded by transportation network changes—creates a unique hardship that can be remedied by allowing indoor adaptive reuse without endorsing the unrestricted build-out of the adjacent undeveloped land. State Requirement: The strict application of the terms of the Zoning Ordinance will constitute an unnecessary hardship if applied to the property for which a variance is sought. Strict enforcement of the Corridor Overlay District (COD) prohibition against vehicle sales and service would prevent the economic reuse of a purpose-built, 2.04-acre commercial site (Lot 3) that already possesses the necessary building footprint and pavement. Forcing this established building to remain vacant—particularly after state-initiated access closures reduced passerby traffic—imposes an unnecessary economic hardship. Allowing the requested use inside the existing structure relieves this hardship while preserving the Board's discretion to apply strict development standards or limitations on the undeveloped Lot 4 to prevent unnecessary visual appearance. 9 State Requirement: The approval does not interfere substantially with the Comprehensive Plan. The I-69 Corridor Plan explicitly encourages economic vitality and the adaptive reuse of existing commercial inventory impacted by I-69 access modifications along secondary frontage roads. While the plan seeks to prevent the uncontrolled proliferation of roadside vehicle lots along the corridor, permitting the adaptive reuse of the existing structure on Lot 3 directly fulfills the plan's economic revitalization goals. By capping the intensity of the use and enforcing strict design and buffering standards on any proposed staging on Lot 4, the approval honors both the plan's economic goals and its intent to elevate the visual gateway standards of Johnson County.. PROPERTY DESCRIPTION This 2.56-acre site is zoned SR (Single-Family Residential) and is currently improved with a single-family dwelling and one accessory structure. The area surrounding this parcel consists of parcels of similar size, all used residentially. The properties directly to the west are located within the municipal limits of the town of Bargersville. VARIANCE REQUEST – DEVELOPMENT STANDARD The applicant is requesting a Variance of Development Standard to allow the construction of a 2,952-square-foot accessory structure on the subject property. The site currently contains two accessory structures: a 1,440-square-foot detached garage and a 96-square-foot shed. With the addition of the proposed 2,952-square-foot building, the total aggregate area of all three accessory structures would be 4,488 square feet. This exceeds the square footage of the primary dwelling, which is 2,912 square feet. The zoning ordinance stipulates that the total aggregate area of all accessory structures on a single lot shall not exceed 100% of the square footage of the primary dwelling (proposed at ~154%). items.text: pg. 1 JOHNSON COUNTY Department of Planning & Zoning Phone: (317) 346-4350 86 West Court Street www.co.johnson.in.us Franklin, Indiana 46131 MEETING AGENDA Johnson County Advisory Plan Commission August 24th, 2026 - 6:00 PM Public Auditorium, West Annex Building 86 West Court Street, Franklin, Indiana CALL TO ORDER ROLL CALL APPROVAL of MINUTES Approval of minutes from the March 23, 2026 meeting. OTHER APPOINTMENTS PUBLIC HEARINGS -CONTINUED HEARINGS- -NEW HEARINGS – W-3-26 Coy Waiver, 3131 S 350 W, Trafalgar WAIVER of the Johnson County Unified Development Ordinance to provide for a potential two-lot Minor Subdivision with one of the lots having a depth-to-width ratio of 2.2:1 Unified Development Ordinance Amendments – The proposed changes cover key operational areas including statutory protections for shooting ranges, defined standards for event centers and group homes, clarification of accessory dwelling unit and structure sizes, and relief from suburban standards (such as sidewalks and individual lot landscaping) in rural and agricultural zoning districts. OLD BUSINESS NEW BUSINESS REPORTS and RECOMMENDATIONS pg. 2 ADJOURNMENT The next meeting of the Johnson County Advisory Plan Commission is scheduled for September 28th, 2026 at 6:00 PM in the public auditorium of the Courthouse West Annex Building. LIVE STREAMING AVAILABLE HERE Meeting ID: 853 5483 6693 Passcode: 057410 (Link can also be found on the County Website under Events Calendar – Click on Events Website) In accordance with American Disabilities Act, any person attending the public meeting in need of reasonable accommodations in order to attend, hear, or present evidence at the public meeting on an agenda item should contact the Johnson County ADA coordinator, Barb Davis, at 86 W. Court St., Franklin, IN 46131, (317) 346-4329, bdavis@co.johnson.in.us. Pursuant to Indiana Code 5-14-9 (the “Act”), board member terms and appointing authority: Johnson County Plan Commission Appointment Member Appointing Authority Term Ron West Representative County Commissioner 1/1/2026 - 12/31/2026 Jonathan T. Myers Representative County Council 1/1/2026 - 12/31/2026 Ron Bates Alternate Member - County Council 1/1/2026 - 12/31/2026 Greg Cantwell Surveyor - Office Held Office Term Shalee Bradley ANR County Extension Agent - Office Held Office Term Charles Canary Citizen Member appointed by County Commissioners 1/1/2023 - 12/31/2027 Douglas Gray Citizen Member appointed by County Commissioners 1/1/2024 - 12/31/2027 Steven Hickman Citizen Member appointed by County Commissioners 1/1/2023 - 12/31/2027 Robert Page Citizen Member appointed by County Commissioners 1/1/2024 - 12/31/2027 Stoney Vann Citizen Member appointed by County Commissioners 1/1/2025 - 12/31/2028 Staff Report CASE NUMBER: W-3-26, Coy Waiver ADDRESS: 3131 S 350 W, Trafalgar PETITIONER: Dale & Jacqueline Coy by Barkocy Surveying, Inc REQUEST WAIVER of the Johnson County Unified Development Ordinance to provide for a potential two-lot Minor Subdivision with one of the lots having a depth-to-width ratio of 2.2:1 (in Minor Subdivisions, lots with an area less than five acres may have a depth-to-width ratio no greater than 2:1) STAFF RECOMMENDATION Staff recommends approval of this request. PROPERTY DESCRIPTION The subject property is 7.2 acres parcel in Hensley Township. The site is zoned SR (Single-Family Residential) and is currently improved with a single-family dwelling and a few accessory structures. The parcel is bordered by larger track of land used agriculturally. WAIVER REQUEST The petitioners are requesting a waiver from the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) subdivision lot arrangement standards to create a two-lot minor subdivision.  Lot 1: Proposed at 2.00 acres, containing an existing residential dwelling.  Lot 2: Proposed at 4.92 acres, containing existing accessory structures, mature trees, and a driveway. Per the UDO, lots under 5.0 acres in size are required to maintain a maximum depth-to-width ratio of 2:1.  Intent of Standard: The depth-to-width ratio requirement is designed to prevent "bowling alley" or "flag shape" lots, ensuring that parcels maintain functional, buildable proportions rather than overly narrow configurations. It discourages irregular lot boundaries designed solely to satisfy dimensional metrics on paper, promoting straightforward, clean lot lines that simplify property maintenance, access, and land ownership disputes over time. Lot 1: Meets all UDO lot ratio and dimensional standards. Lot 2: At 4.92 acres, Lot 2 falls just 0.08 acres short of the 5-acre threshold where depth-to-width standards no longer apply. The proposed lot measures 280 feet in width by 615 feet in depth, resulting in a depth-to-width ratio of 2.2 to 1. Staff Analysis & Findings To satisfy the strict 2:1 ratio (requiring a minimum lot width of ~307.5 feet for a 615-foot depth), the applicant evaluated an alternate layout. That compliant layout would require an artificial "bump-out" into Lot 1 near the road frontage (extending width to 307 feet for approximately 40 feet) before narrowing back down. Staff finds that strict compliance via this alternate layout creates undesirable planning outcomes:  It introduces an irregular property line configuration solely to satisfy a technical metric on paper.  It causes the shared property line to intersect existing site improvements, including an established driveway and mature tree line, necessitating unnecessary cross-access or boundary easements. Granting the requested waiver to allow a 2.2:1 ratio allows for a clean, straight interior lot line that keeps existing site features intact on Lot 2 without creating awkward lot geometries along the public road frontage. The deviation from the standard is minor (2.2:1 vs 2:1) and presents no adverse impacts on surrounding properties, public safety, or traffic flow. FINDINGS OF FACT, STAFF ANALYSIS The granting of the waiver will not be detrimental to the public safety, health, or welfare or be injurious to nearby property; The granting of this waiver will not be detrimental to public safety, health, or welfare, nor will it be injurious to nearby properties. The requested depth-to-width ratio adjustment applies solely to an internal lot configuration (Lot 2) and will not negatively impact surrounding properties, public safety, or existing public infrastructure. The waiver requested will not affect the area adjacent to the property in a substantially adverse manner because: The requested waiver is a minor numeric deviation (a 2.2:1 ratio vs. the required 2:1 ratio) on a 4.92-acre lot that falls just 0.08 acres short of the 5-acre threshold where the rule no longer applies. The adjustment does not increase density, alter permitted land uses, or change the rural character of the immediate area. The conditions upon which the request for a waiver are based are unique to the property for which the waiver is sought and are not applicable generally to other properties. The subject parcel features long-established physical improvements, including an existing driveway and mature tree line serving Lot 2. Designing a fully compliant 2:1 lot would require introducing irregular "jogs" or a temporary bump-out along the road frontage, creating unnecessary cross-boundary encumbrances that are unique to this specific site layout. The strict application of the terms of the Unified Development Ordinance will result in unnecessary hardship because: Strict application of the UDO ratio would force the applicant to place the shared lot line through the existing driveway and mature trees. This would require creating unnecessary cross-access and maintenance easements between the two parcels. Alternatively, forcing a compliant 2:1 lot width near the road frontage results in an irregular, unnatural property line configuration solely to satisfy a paper metric. The waiver is not primarily for the economic benefit of the petitioner because: The request is strictly driven by sound land planning principles to achieve a logical, straight-line property boundary that keeps existing physical improvements (driveway and trees) entirely on the lot they serve. The waiver request is not due to a hardship caused by the current owner of the property. The existing driveway and mature tree lines predate the current owner's acquisition of the land. The hardship stems from adapting an established residential site to modern UDO dimensional standards rather than any recent action taken by the petitioner. The waiver will not, in any manner, contravene provisions of the Zoning Ordinance, Comprehensive Plan, or Official Map, as interpreted by the Commission. The proposed minor subdivision complies with all underlying zoning standards, including minimum lot area, lot width, and setback requirements for both proposed lots. The request represents a slight numerical variance (2.2:1 vs. 2:1) on a parcel that is only 0.08 acres short of the 5-acre threshold where depth-to-width limits cease to apply. Approval of the waiver aligns with the Comprehensive Plan by encouraging orderly growth, preserving existing site improvements, and avoiding irregular property geometries along public rights-of-way. GENERAL INFORMATION Subdivider: Dale and Jacquline Coy 3131 S 350 W Trafalgar IN 46181 Owner: Same Current Zoning: SR Single Family Residential Existing Land Use: Single-family residential Future Land Use: Rural Residential -MNH W-3-26 Base Map Subject Site W-3-26 Base Map II W-3-26 SUBJECT PROPERTY W-3-26 Petitioner’s Findings of Facts © 2026 Microsoft Corporation © Maxar ©CNES (2026) Distribution Airbus DS © 2026 TMAP MOBILITY Earthstar Geographics SIO © Mapbox 4800 West Smith Valley Road, Suite O * Greenwood, IN 46142 Office - 317-881-3898 * www.BarkocySurveying.com BARKOCY W N E S S U R V E Y I N G I N C . professional land surveying & land development services 4800 West Smith Valley Road, Suite O * Greenwood, IN 46142 Office - 317-881-3898 * www.BarkocySurveying.com BARKOCY W N E S S U R V E Y I N G I N C . professional land surveying & land development services UNIFIED DEVELOPMENT ORDINANCE – 2026 Amendment proposal The Department of Planning and Zoning has prepared a series of proposed text amendments to the Johnson County Uniﬁed Development Ordinance (UDO). Following the comprehensive adoption of the UDO in 2024, staff have identiﬁed several areas requiring technical cleanup, administrative clariﬁcation, and legislative updates. The proposed changes cover key operational areas including statutory protections for shooting ranges, deﬁned standards for event centers and group homes, clariﬁcation of accessory dwelling unit and structure sizes, and relief from suburban standards (such as sidewalks and individual lot landscaping) in rural and agricultural zoning districts.  Draft Redline Version of UDO Amendments as of 8-14-26  List of track changes to the UDO Shooting / Archery Range – Indoor Rationale: Amendments were incorporated pursuant to Senate Enrolled Act (SEA) 176, which establishes protections for existing shooting ranges to ensure they may continue operating without being subject to non-conforming restrictions when modiﬁed. The legislation also mandates that shooting ranges and sporting goods stores be permitted by right in designated zoning districts, subject to speciﬁc conditions. Affected Sections: Pages 15, 17, 27, 29, 31, 115, 246, and Appendix A. Event Centers Rationale: Event centers (deﬁned as facilities hosted for private gatherings, parties, celebrations, and family events) were added as a distinct, described land use within the UDO. Staff routinely receives inquiries regarding this use, but the ordinance previously lacked clear operational guidance and dimensional standards. This amendment deﬁnes "Event Center" and establishes the speciﬁc zoning districts where the use is permitted. Affected Sections: Pages 15, 27, 29, 236, and Appendix A. Accessory Dwelling Units. Rationale: Proposed revisions to the Accessory Dwelling Unit standards provide clarity and prevent unintentional misinterpretation: Density Limits: Attached and detached ADUs were previously listed separately, with individual provisions stating a quantity of "one" was permitted. To prevent interpretations that a single property could construct both an attached and a detached ADU, the word "or detached/attached" was inserted to clarify that only one ADU type is permitted per lot. Addressing Standards: Revised the addressing provision to clarify that obtaining a distinct address for an ADU is optional (upon request by the property owner) rather than mandatory. Affected Sections: Page 93. Accessory Structure Rationale: Prior to the 2024 UDO adoption, the county ordinance regulated accessory structures based on the aggregate square footage of all structures on a lot. This provision was incorrectly converted during the 2024 update, leading to conﬂicting interpretations. The proposed text restores the original intent by clarifying that the combined gross ﬂoor area of all accessory structures on a parcel shall not exceed the designated size threshold. Affected Sections: Page 95. Group Home and Nursing Homes Rationale: Updates were made to the group home standards to align county zoning regulations better with ADA and federal fair housing guidelines, while resolving internal code inconsistencies across residential zoning districts. Deﬁnition & Scale: The UDO explicitly distinguishes a Group Home from larger institutional facilities, such as commercial nursing or convalescent centers. This distinction ensures group homes operate within a typical residential scale and character. State Compliance: Standards were updated to reference appropriate state licensing bodies—speciﬁcally the Division of Disability and Rehabilitative Services (DDRS) and the Division of Mental Health and Addiction (DMHA)—ensuring local oversight supports, rather than conﬂicts with, state licensing mandates. Permitted Districts & Occupancy Caps: Clariﬁed standards across residential and agricultural districts. Occupancy remains capped at eight (8) residents (excluding support staff) to maintain compatibility with single-family residential neighborhoods while ensuring compliance with federal Fair Housing Act protections for group living arrangements. Permitting & Review Process: Streamlined the review framework to clarify when a facility is permitted by right versus when it requires special approval, eliminating previous ambiguity surrounding unlisted uses or special exception requirements for state-licensed residential care homes. Affected Sections: Pages 15, 17,,19,21,23,27 105, 112,236,238,240, and Appendix A. Minimum Development Size for Commercial and Industrial Land Rationale: The 2024 UDO update introduced a minimum acreage threshold for commercial and industrial developments. Upon reviewing recent major plat ﬁlings and waiver requests, Staff identiﬁed that most existing commercial and industrial parcels in the county do not meet this minimum acreage requirement and are not adjacent to parcels that could be combined to meet it. While encouraging coordinated, large-scale development is ideal, this standard inadvertently prevents viable property divisions on smaller lots and is uncommonly restrictive compared to peer jurisdictions. Staff recommends deleting this requirement. Affected Sections: Pages 128 and 129. Deﬁnitions added Rationale: Restored deﬁnitions from the 2002 Zoning Ordinance to better deﬁne "front yard" and "lot lines" for setback calculations. Additionally, modiﬁed the general setback deﬁnition to clarify that setback regulations apply to all structures, not just primary buildings. Minor Text Amendments & Technical Fixes Page 38 (I-69 Corridor Overlay Setback): Re-established the I-69 setback requirement within the Corridor Overlay District. The prior zoning ordinance was drafted before Interstate 69 was constructed, and this overlay provision was inadvertently omitted during the 2024 UDO adoption. Pages 67–68 (Individual Lot Landscaping): Removed individual lot landscaping requirements for Agricultural (A) and Agricultural-Residential (A-R) zoned properties. These standards are intended for major/minor residential subdivisions rather than rural, agricultural acreage. Page 87 (Inoperable Vehicle Storage): Reverted inoperable vehicle storage standards for A and A-R districts back to pre-2024 regulations (allowing one inoperable vehicle per property without full screening requirements). The 2024 UDO requirement for complete visual screening will now apply primarily to suburban and commercial districts, aligning with county policy prioritizing reduced enforcement in rural areas. Page 130 (Sidewalk Requirements): Removed mandatory sidewalk installation for minor subdivisions. Because the majority of minor subdivisions occur in rural areas where sidewalk networks do not exist, this requirement routinely resulted in unnecessary waiver requests.
