items.title: Town of Whiteland: Board of Zoning Appeals
items.text:
The Whiteland Advisory Board of Zoning Appeals (“BZA”) works to ensure that zoning regulations are fairly applied across varying properties in town. Essentially, the BZA serves as a board to hear appeals that specific zoning regulations should be applied differently to a particular property due to certain conditions of the site or the proposed use. The administrative appeal is an appeal of a decision made by town staff regarding the zoning code. The BZA does not enforce the zoning code, but they can adjust the regulations for a property to suit its specific site conditions that would otherwise be in violation of the zoning code. The responsibilities of the BZA is as follows:
Indiana Code provides that the BZA has the following specific authorities:
Granting of variances Developmental standards variances Variances of use
Developmental standards variances
Variances of use
Granting of special exceptions (also known as conditional uses)
Appeals from administrative decisions
Members
Two members of the BZA are selected from the Plan Commission, two are appointed by the Town Council President, and one is appointed by the Town Council. By state code, members cannot hold any other elected or appointed position (except the two Plan Commission members).

CGHS Pick-Up/Drop Off
Directions to CGHS
CGHS Daily/Event Parking
Traffic routes around the Center Grove High School have been updated for the 2025-26 school year. These changes are designed to improve safety, reduce traffic back-up on Morgantown Road, and improve traffic flow - based on feedback we received last year.
STUDENT DROP-OFF AND PICK-UP Parents dropping off and picking up students from Center Grove High School should enter the high school campus by turning off of Morgantown Road onto Pennington Drive. Traffic on Pennington will continue through the peanut-shaped roundabout to east of the Tennis Complex and into the lot between the Innovation Center and Baseball Field. (See map below.) Parents will then continue north through the lot to the exit and turn left (south) back onto Trojan Lane. They will travel west, past the Tennis Complex, and turn right (north) onto Victory Lane to enter the drop-off/pick-up line. Drop-off is at Door #9, the same as prior years. This is the only location where students should be dropped off at school. Parents will then exit the campus by following Victory Lane to the roundabout at the intersection with Trojan Lane and continue north to Stones Crossing Road.
STUDENT PARKING FOOTBALL STUDENT LOT: Students may enter the parking lot east of the football stadium from Morgantown Road. They should take Pennington Road straight through the peanut-shaped roundabout, and curve around to Trojan Lane. There is no access from the north on Trojan Lane before school to this lot. This is not a change from prior years, however, students will be permitted to exit via Morgantown or Stones Crossing after school this year. Please note that this traffic will merge at the roundabout with parent pick-up traffic and students exiting the north lots.
NORTH STUDENT LOTS: Students may enter the north student lots from Stones Crossing Road. They should turn onto Trojan Lane and turn right into the student lot. (This is not a change from prior years.) GATE RESTRICTIONS Gates will be down on Pennington Road at the peanut to restrict traffic from turning left onto Victory Lane and on Trojan Lane just south of the roundabout from 7:30-8:05 AM when school is in session. The Pennington Road gate will also be down from 2:15-3:15 PM.
DURING SCHOOL PICK-UP AND DROP-OFF During the school day, students who are dropped off and picked up for appointments or late arrivals should use Door #9 (Hall of Excellence), where they will check in with staff at the security vestibule. After 1:30 PM, students may be picked up for appointments from Door #1should use the front administrative entrance (Door #1) at the flagpole/electronic sign off of Morgantown Road. Parents who need to come into the building should also use Door #1.
AFTER SCHOOL ACTIVITY DROP-OFF AND PICK-UP Parents dropping off and picking up students of any age for activities at Center Grove High School must follow the traffic markings around the high school.

JACK RUSSELL President, CGCSC Board of School Trustees
Jack Russell is a long-time resident of the Center Grove community. He graduated from Center Grove High School in 1974. He is a graduate of Purdue University where he studied Elementary Education. After Purdue, Mr. Russell attended Butler University to study dance and acting.
Russell spent time traveling the country after graduation doing live shows at theme parks and dinner theaters. During that time, he would also substitute teach in the local school system. After a few years working as general manager in his family’s real estate and development business, Russell returned to the world of education to teach full-time. He also spent time substitute teaching while raising his son, Austin, whom he adopted from Paraguay. Austin is a 2013 Center Grove graduate.
Russell has been an active member of the Center Grove Education Foundation. He is also involved with the Center Grove Alumni and Friends group. Russell was elected to the Center Grove Board of School Trustees in 2010 and has served in various leadership positions, including as president in 2013.
SCOTT ALEXANDER Vice President, CGCSC Board of School Trustees
Scott Alexander is a 1991 graduate of Center Grove High School and a lifelong Center Grove resident. He received his bachelor’s degree from Purdue University in 1995. Mr. Alexander is the Vice President, of Sales and Strategic Partnerships for InTempo Software.
Alexander joined Center Grove’s Board of School Trustees in 2010. Prior to that he was a four-year member of the Center Grove Education Foundation.
Alexander's Information Technology background spans over the past 18 years with experience in various leadership roles. He has spent a large portion of his career in the pharmaceutical and healthcare industries with some experience in consulting as well. Alexander brings vast experience in leading teams and businesses of varying sizes through information technology, operations, and logistics.
Alexander and his wife, Dana, have two sons who are graduates of Center Grove High School. In his spare time, he enjoys playing golf.
JANE DUNIGAN-SMITH Secretary, CGCSC Board of School Trustees
Jane Dunigan-Smith has lived in the Center Grove community for more than 22 years. She is the Senior Vice President and Chief Strategy Officer at BioCrossroads. Dunigan-Smith has a master’s degree in business administration, marketing and strategy and a bachelor’s degree in accounting and finance from the Kelley School of Business at Indiana University, Bloomington.
Dunigan-Smith has served on the Board of the Center Grove Education Foundation and is a graduate of the Center Grove Ambassadors program. She and her husband, Rodney, have two sons, one graduate of Center Grove High School (CGHS) and a senior at CGHS.

Greenwood has undertaken several redevelopment projects in Old Town recently as it continues revitalization of the city’s downtown and surrounding areas.
Most recently, the Greenwood Redevelopment Commission (RDC) approved a project agreement between the city, CRG Residential and Great Lakes Capital to redevelop the former Greenwood Middle School property.

$83 million total investment
2.5 year construction timeline, which began in 2021

items.text: Meeting of the Greenwood Common Council ROLL CALL Date: September 21, 2026 Time: 7:00 pm Place: Council Chamber 300 S Madison Ave Greenwood, Indiana I. Call Meeting to Order A. Pledge of Allegiance B. Prayer: David Denny - lay leader at Victory Baptist Church C. Roll Call: Council Members Present: Mike Campbell ("Mr. Campbell"), Linda Gibson ("Ms. Gibson"), Ezra Hill ("Mr. Hill"), David Hopper ("Mr. Hopper"), Erin Kasch ("Ms. Kasch"), David Lekse, ("Mr. Lekse"), Teri Manship, ("Ms. Manship"), Steve Moan ("Mr. Moan") Darin Hoggatt ("Mr. Hoggatt") City Officials: Mark Myers (“Mayor Myers”) Jeannine Myers ("Ms. Myers") Clerk, Greg Wright ("Mr. Wright") Controller, Sam Hodson (“Mr. Hodson”) Corporation Council, James Ison ("Chief Ison") Police Chief, Jayme Washel (“Chief Washel”) Fire Chief, and Department Heads. Council President Campbell reminded attendees that respectful participation is expected and that disruptions are not permitted. This will be read before each meeting: Before we begin, I want to remind everyone that respectful participation is expected. We welcome public input but there will be no yelling or interruptions that prevent the meeting from moving forward. Anyone who disrupts the meeting will be asked to leave and may be escorted out. II. Approval of Minutes A. Minutes from the regular meeting September 9 ,2026 Motion to approve regular meeting minutes from September 9, 2026 by Kasch, seconded by Hill Votes: Ayes – Campbell, Gibson, Hill, Hopper Kasch Abstain: Lekse, Manship, Moan, Hoggatt Motion Passes: 5-0 with 4 abstentions III. Reports A. Corporation Counsel B. Controller C. Committee & Board Report IV. Public Comments This timeslot is for residents who would like to address the Council about matters on the agenda. All materials presented at a public meeting are considered part of the official record; please provide a copy to the Clerk. Individuals- 5-minute time limit; Groups- 20-minute time limit V. Ordinances and Resolutions A. Notice of Intent to Consider ORDINANCE NO. 26-24 AN ORDINANCE TO AMEND THE OFFICIAL ZONING MAP ADOPTED BY REFERENCE IN UNIFIED DEVELOPMENT ORDINANCE NO. 20-29 (PROPOSED REZONING OF APPROXIMATELY 80.15 ACRES LOCATED ON THE SOUTHEAST CORNER OF I-65 AND WORTHSVILLE ROAD (Sponsors Campbell, Gibson, Hopper, Lekse and Manship) Motion to amend Ord. No. 26-24 PD7.12.1 (d) pre-cast concrete panels shall not exceed an area more than 80% of the front elevation. motion by Lekse seconded by Hopper Votes: Ayes - Campbell, Gibson, Hill, Hopper, Kasch, Lekse, Manship, Moan, Hoggatt Motion passes: 9-0 Motion to pass Ord. No. 26-24 as amended by Hopper, seconded by Gibson Votes: Ayes - Campbell, Gibson, Hopper, Kasch, Lekse, Manship, Moan Nays – Hill, Hoggatt Motion passes: 7-2 B. First Reading ORDINANCE NO. 26-29 AN ORDINANCE OF THE COMMON COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF GREENWOOD, INDIANA, AUTHORIZING AND ESTABLISHING THE BOUNDARIES OF FOUR MUNICIPAL RIVERFRONT DEVELOPMENT PROJECT AREAS WITHIN THE CITY OF GREENWOOD PURSUANT TO INDIANA CODE §7.1-3-20-16 AND INDIANA CODE §7.1-3-20-16.1 (Sponsored by Hill, Manship) Motion to pass Ord. No. 26-24 by Hopper, seconded by Gibson Votes: Ayes - Campbell, Gibson, Hill, Hoggatt, Hopper, Kasch, Lekse, Manship, Moan Motion passes: 9-0 C. Second Reading VI. New Business – Introductions of New Ordinances and Resolutions ORDINANCE NO. 26-30 AN ORDINANCE FIXING THE SALARY OF THE COMMON COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF GREENWOOD, INDIANA FOR THE YEAR 2027 (Sponsored by Gibson, Kasch) ORDINANCE NO. 26-31 AN ORDINANCE FIXING THE SALARY OF THE MAYOR OF THE CITY OF GREENWOOD, INDIANA FOR THE YEAR 2027 (Sponsored by Gibson, Kasch) ORDINANCE NO. 26-32 AN ORDINANCE FIXING THE SALARY OF THE CLERK OF THE CITY OF GREENWOOD, INDIANA FOR THE YEAR 2027 (Sponsored by Gibson, Kasch) ORDINANCE NO. 26-33 AN ORDINANCE FIXING THE SALARY OF THE CITY JUDGE OF THE CITY OF GREENWOOD, INDIANA FOR THE YEAR 2027(Sponsored by Gibson, Kasch) ORDINANCE NO. 26-34 AN ORDINANCE FIXING SALARIES OF APPOINTED OFFICERS AND EMPLOYEES OF THE CITY OF GREENWOOD, INDIANA AND CITY UTILITIES FOR THE YEAR 2027 (Sponsored by Gibson, Kasch) ORDINANCE NO. 26-35 AN ORDINANCE FOR APPROPRIATIONS AND TAX RATES FOR THE 2027 BUDGET YEAR (Sponsored by Gibson, Kasch) Public Hearing scheduled for October 5, 2026 RESOLUTION NO. 26-09 A RESOLUTION DECLARING CERTAIN REAL PROPERTY IMPROVEMENTS FOR TAX ABATEMENT (Exeter Southtech Land, LLC- EQT Southtech Building 1) (Sponsored by Gibson) VII. Miscellaneous Business A. Public Comments This timeslot is for residents who would like to address the Council about matters not on the agenda. All materials presented at a public meeting are considered part of the official record; please provide a copy to the Clerk. Individuals- 5-minute time limit; Groups- 20-minute time limit. B. Council 1. Greenwood BTS Motion to find Greenwood BTS not in compliance by Hopper, seconded by Lekse Votes: All Ayes C. Other Miscellaneous A. Corporation Counsel B. Controller C. Mayor VIII. Please allow at least two business days to arrange for accommodations. Individuals- 5-minute time limit; Groups- 20-minute time limit Deann Lautenbach, 2255 S. Franklin Rd, Greenwood, IN 46143 I live at the corner of Franklin and Clark Road in Greenwood. I'm an aggravated and affected neighbor due to living in the middle of the unfinished corridor between 65 and 74, which will be feeding an enormous amount of traffic to the destination travel center, being one of the largest gas stations in the entire state of Indiana. I am here tonight to establish a formal legally binding administrative record against docket PC 2026-035. To fully preserve my right to file a judicial review in the Johnson County courts. I request that this Council table this back to the Planning Commission or deny this petition because it creates a severe procedural violation, breaks local ordinances, and creates a textbook, arbitrary, capricious action. Indiana open door law. Under Indiana Code Section 5.14 1.55, public agencies are required to give public notice of their meetings, including posting an agenda if one is utilized at least 48 hours in advance, excluding weekends and legal holidays, dropping a major, unvetted, supplemental traffic study on a Friday afternoon for a Monday vote, actively circumvents the transparency mandated by the state sunshine law. Greenwood Planning Division staff report ruled: after an examination of information in the public record and findings from additional research, staff shall publish a technical review committee report that provides an analysis of the petition request. Such reports shall be published along with an agenda approximately five days prior to the meeting. By failing to give a five-day buffer, the city directly broke its own local guidelines. Indiana Code Section 3674607. This statute dictates that any zoning ordinance or planned unit development text amendment must follow a strict process between the Planning Commission and the Legislative Council. Under Indiana Land Use law, if a developer introduces significant technical updates or modifications after the Planning Commission has already voted, the Common Council is legally required to remand the proposal back to the Planning Commission. This ensures that the public hearing body can officially investigate, review, and certify the new data before a final vote takes place. Indiana Code Section 3674604. This statute mandates that a major zoning ordinance or text amendment cannot be legally enacted without a formal, legally advertised public hearing because the brand-new September 15th traffic memo reveals a severe level of service F gridlock. Failures right at our local school entrances, avenues, and because this data was hidden from the public portal until Friday afternoon, the community has never been granted a valid public hearing on the actual material facts of this case. I gave you guys all exhibits. Exhibit A: The build, this is from the traffic study, build 2037 capacity reports from Section F, all the traffic study. This document proves that the intersection of Emerson Avenue and Worthsville Road will suffer complete gridlock during peak morning school hours. The northbound approach drops to a level of service grade F, forcing parents, teachers, and school buses to face a catastrophic average delay of 275.26 seconds, which is over four and a half minutes. Of forced idling per vehicle. This extensive line of cars will stack directly backward during the morning peak hour, clogging the entrance avenues of Clark Pleasant Middle School and creating a dangerous hazard gridlock where student commuters are trapped in stationary traffic. Exhibit B: The existing 2026 plus site capacity reports from Section D of the study. This proves that the infrastructure will fail on day one. The very moment this site opens, page two reveals that the southbound approach directly exiting the Grassy Creek Elementary School access road completely breaks down into an immediate level of service F, forcing parents and school buses to idle for 74.9 seconds, over a minute each just to exit the school gates. Furthermore, page four exposed a catastrophic four-way systematic breakdown at county roads. 200 East and Worthsville Road, where the northbound and southbound approaches simultaneously fail at level service F, blocking up primary school access road with immediate delays up to three and a half minutes. Exhibit C, and I have more, but I can't. proving the developers actively breaking our local laws to circumvent safety protections, unifying development ordinances section 100107 with the illegal spot zoning. That's going on. I need to put that in the record so I can file a judicial review. Furthermore, your master plan used on table 17 completely bans travel plazas. That is illegal spot zoning. The developer is also proposing to remove an active timed travel traffic signal along the corridor and replace it with a roundabout element, eliminating the only mechanical guarantee that stops commercial traffic to let parents in school buses. Thank you. Kim Crawford, 166 Caplinger Place, Greenwood, In 46143 I am also the school board president for the Clark Pleasant Community School Corporation. Council President, Council Members, and City staff, thank you for the opportunity to speak this evening. I am here on behalf of the Clark Pleasant Community School Corporations and the families we serve. We appreciate the city and Buc-ee’s for conducting an initial traffic study and for sharing the updated remote this last week. We're not opposed to the development. However, we do have significant concerns about what the updated study demonstrates and the limited scope of the proposed mitigations. Our responsibility is to ensure that any changes along Worthsville Road support safe, reliable operations for our students, families, and our bus drivers. The updated Buc-ee’s traffic study provides new data on projected traffic volumes and interception performance during school drop-off and pickup windows. Although the city concludes that the site “does not result in significant additional traffic impacts during school- related peak periods,” several findings, including our own observations, indicate meaningful concerns for school operations and student safety. First, school peak traffic is already operating at a near rush-hour intensity. PM drop-off volumes are only about 50 vehicles lower than evening rush-hour peak. Because these peaks do not overlap, Buc-ee’s traffic represents additional load, not shared load. Second, the multiple intersections show significant delay growth between current conditions and 2037 projections. Worthsville and Emerson (northbound) shows substantial increases in delay in the report. Worthsville and Southlake (southbound) already experiences significant drop-off delays and it's projected to nearly double. Worthsville Road and County Road 200 shows delays exceeding 120 seconds or two minutes today- both AM southbound and PM northbound with worsening delays projected. These are the same intersections that our buses and our student drivers and our families use in order to get to the middle school and the two elementary schools there. Third Buc-ee’s is projected to add 1,045 trips during the morning drop-off and 1,380 trips during afternoon pickup. The study attempts to differentiate where these trips go afterwards, but the impact occurs the moment we enter the roadway, Worthsville Road. During compressed school windows, any added volume destabilizes flow. Fourth, only one mitigation has been proposed, re-striving at the southbound approach at Worthsville Road and Ray Crowe Way. And this is the entrance to the middle school. No other improvements have been recommended for intersections already showing severe delays. If striking Ray Crowe Way was the solution, we would have thought about it and would have done it before now. Finally, despite these findings, the study concludes that Buc-ee's does not result in significant additional traffic impacts during school-related periods. This conclusion does not align with the data that was presented or with school-specific traffic behavior. Because of these concerns, the district respectfully requests a formal commitment from the city and Buc-ee’s. If Buc-ee's operations create significant negative impact on our instructional day, bus routing our on-time performance, or parent pickup and drop-off operations, we just asking that the city and Buc-ee’s re-engage with us collaboratively to identify and implement mitigation strategies, including additional studies or infrastructure improvements. There's very little we can do on our own without more help. Our focus is simple: to ensure that the daily experience of our students, families, and staff remains safe and predictable as this progress progresses. We value our partnership with the city and Buc- ee’s and we want to continue to work together constructively. Thank you for your time and attention. Tim Edsell, Clark-Pleasant School Superintendent Appreciate your leadership. Again, I appreciate a couple of you who met with me individually. Appreciate you listening. I appreciate Scott Ratcliffe, who is one of the senior engineers for Buc-ee’s, for producing the revised traffic study. To me and to us as a school corporation last week. I appreciate them willing to redo the traffic study that last week of August. President Crawford just said a lot of similar points. I'll reiterate a few of them, but not to be repetitive and for the sake of brevity. I do want to emphasize some of those key areas that are of concern to us with the traffic flow That would be Worthsville & Emerson, Worthsville & South Lake Avenue, and Worthsville & County Rd 200 The one suggestion to obviously reach strike the left and turn lanes that's on our property right by middle school entrance. Appreciate that. We could do that. Signage, we could do that. My final request would be: as Buc-ee’s is built, I would love to see improved and stronger communication from all entities because, as it's built and even as it opens up, whatever that timeframe is, and the impact that it will have on our school day is so significant. I would love to work together with, again, all entities because it's important that obviously we conduct school. I've made our Department of Education aware of this. And so, the goal is for us, to work with you, not to be against you, but to make sure that we have school every single day within the required hours that were allotted. Thank you for your time. Mitch Hunter. I live at 3114 East 700 North in Whiteland, Indiana, 46184. Updating the comprehensive plan involves not only community input, hiring the third-party companies of HWC Engineering and Stantec. The project siphoned $200,000 from the city budget. The goal was for the final project to be “the blueprint for the future.” The land in question tonight falls in a major part of that blueprint, one the city deemed worthy of developing a specific vision for how the area will be used and what it would look like in the years to come (Greenwood Crossing). The plan says it is critical that this area holds a strong set of development criteria to ensure new development allows the city to grow its tax base, of course, but also to protect adjacent rural lifestyles. The new plan acknowledges Greenwood residents expressed their concern throughout the process about industrial development continuing south past Worthsville Road. Additionally, the HWC Steering Committee held a meeting specifically addressing the future land use of this area. The very first bullet point meeting states: “Areas surrounding the I-65 and Worthsville Road interchange should remain largely residential with limited commercial uses that serve the surrounding neighborhoods and not those traveling along the highway.” There are two major issues regarding this land and its proposed use. First, the community repeatedly expressed its concern about industrial and warehouse development in the area. Similar projects in the area have not come to fruition because the city listened to the residents and honored their promise to prevent industrial developments. But it's important to note that the problem with proposed industrial developments in the past was not with the business of logistics itself. Rather, it is what those businesses bring to the land: massive structures, invasive lighting, and daunting amounts of traffic. Though not in the business of logistics, a Buc-ee’s brings all of those things front and center, industrial or not. Even though they themselves clearly thought that their operations warranted industrial classifications when they originally brought this before the APC. The spirit of no warehouses and no industrial was to guard against these types of developments. Secondly, allowing this development or any like it will destroy the vision for Greenwood Crossing. The plan calls for a development that is harmonious with residential development on adjacent properties. However, a 120-pump gas station is a poisoned pill. It spoils the land around it. Here is a visual of 37 Buc-ee’s across the United States. I emailed this to each of you earlier. Thank you for those that responded, confirming that you received it. What it shows here is there's a radius of 2,500 feet from the proposed site. The distance that in our plan is supposed to be residential. And when you look at that, you will see that there is no new housing development in any of those 37. Maybe some was existing, but nothing new. All that comes afterwards is warehouses and other large-scale development buildings. Every Buc-ee’s dead zone is a far cry from what Greenwood Crossing is supposed to be, from what we spent $200,000 to plan, and from what this Council promised was in our future. Thank You Mike Venatta, 1085 S Nay Rd, Greenwood, retired. We built our house 25 years ago on Nay Road. And I see several things with Buc-ee’s, and I'm not anti-Buc-ee’s. I'm anti-the location of this Buc-ee’s in Greenwood at this particular location. One, it really doesn't bring hundreds of pre-paying jobs. If you look at it close it brings jobs that are almost identical to the warehouse jobs that we've got now in Greenwood. Of the 200 jobs there, five of them would have enough money to buy a medium-sized house in the city of Greenwood. Again, I'm not putting down the job thing. What is important is, I think, what the last gentleman said quite a bit, and the confusion that's out there, if you look, I just got this letter today from INDOT, and it was something I've been requesting. And thank goodness they shared the traffic info with these other people first. But I'm going to read you, if you would, and if you trust an old guy that's 75 years old. What you see on the internet when you pull this up. Last Friday, I did an AI overview request on the I-65 of Worthsville Road Interchange looking for this new study. Here's what I got: the I-65 of Worthsville Road Interchange in Greenwood, Indiana, can handle roughly 23,000 vehicles per day, but traffic data shows it is already pushing its design limits. Daily capacity recent traffic impact studies and local projections highlight that the current volume of 23,000 vehicles daily already causes the interchange to approach or fail standard design levels during peak hours. The diverging diamond interchange, which Mayor Myers bragged about and should have years ago, about taking the load off the south side, keeping traffic moving smoothly. And remember, we have neighbors too, Whiteland, New Whiteland, that are building up like crazy. But it says “this interchange is highly effective at moving traffic efficiently without requiring left turns. However, area growth from local schools, (God bless them), and residential developments has heavily burdened its capacity. Buc-ee’s impact: Travel projections show that adding an estimated 15,000 new daily trips on top of the existing 23,000 vehicles would cause the intersection flow to fail completely. And here's something I want to ask you guys to consider deeply. I'm old, I can watch YouTube, and I love watching that. Here's Indiana, here's the growing counties, here's the growing cities. Greenwood's been on there, and one of the major advantages of Greenwood is being close to Indianapolis. And not having congestion to get there. They have said repeatedly with Fishers and Carmel, I-69 is a mess every morning. So, I want you to consider this, if you would, please. Of the estimated daily vehicles, and this is the breakdown, I guess, the way that Buc-ee’s does it: pass by intercept: 10,500 to 12,000 is existing highway traffic pulling off and returning to I-65. No new cars added. Great. The next one: primary new trips, brand new trips generated to local roads explicitly to visit Buc-ee’s. Think Indianapolis, think Franklin, think Shelbyville, think Bloomington, think everywhere. That the total estimated daily vehicles, and this is non-interstate, is 3000-4500. I'm not a traffic analyst by any means. I'm college educated. I do have 40 years of corporate experience, but don't tell me that Greenwood isn't facing congestion now on holidays and weekends. And how do you explain adding up to 4,500 more cars every day from local roads? It's not going to just affect us on the south side, it's going to affect all of Greenwood. And just please consider that. And plus, I guess to sum up, there's 1,500 homes or residents that are going to be affected, probably lose five to ten percent of their value. Mine's one of them. But that's just me personally. But everyone in Greenwood is going to be affected by the congestion and the other things. So please consider that, thank you for your time. Carmen Manson, 121 South Meridian Street, Greenwood, IN. I am for Buc-ee’s, I have been to 3 states, 4 Buc-ee’s and have never had a problem getting in or out. I've been to one as an open, never had a problem getting in or out. I love Buc-ee’s. I love the food. I love the people. I love the merchandise. I think it would be good for Greenwood. As the back of my shirt says, life is better at Buc-ee’s. I would love to see that sign that says 240 miles to Buc-ee’s to say Greenwood, to Buc-ee’s, to Worthsville Avenue, your next Buc-ee’s. So please vote yes. We want Buc-ee’s. And that's hundreds of people on Facebook next door, Greenwood Chatter, Center Grove Chatter, who have tied in and said, bring it. So, bring it. That takes care of the 20 minutes on Ordinance 26-24. Anyone else here that would like to speak to the council concerning another item that is on tonight’s agenda? If so, please step to the podium and state your name and address. Seeing none and moving on V. Ordinances and Resolutions A. Notice of Intent to Consider Ordinance No. 26-24 An Ordinance to amend the official zoning map adopted by reference and unified development Ordinance number 20-29. Proposed rezoning of approximately 80.15 acres located on the southeast corner of Interstate 65 & Worthsville Road. (Sponsors: Campbell, Gibson, Hopper, Lexi, and Manship) Is there a petitioner here? Good evening, Mr. President, members of the Common Council. My name is Bryan Tuohy. My address is 9294 North Meridian Street, and I'm here representing the petitioner, which is a company called CSMS Management LLC, which is an affiliate of Buc-ee's LLC. Here with me tonight is Scott Ratcliff, the Director of Engineering for Buc-ee’s, Angela Jarvik who's with Buc-ee’s Real Estate Department, Sammy Bijonowski, who's a traffic engineer with Kimley-Horn, and also Chad Mayes, the lead engineer for Kimley-Horn on this development. Thank you for hearing our case. May I make a presentation to the Council? Thank you, sir. So members of the Council, this site is an 80-acre site, as you've heard from some folks that spoke in here tonight. It's at the southeast corner of Worthsville Road and I-65. This first exhibit here shows that the site, there's next to no residential development around that site. To the north of it is a farm store and then a significantly sized, successful industrial park. On the west side of the site is Interstate 65. On the north side of the site is Worthsville Road. On the east side of the site is Collins Rd and County Road 250 East. That makes this site in the corner of this interstate a very attractive site for commercial development because it's bordered by three sides by three roads. When the Council is looking into rezoning one of the elements to look at is what does the comprehensive plan call for in the development of a particular site? And this slide here is from the Greenwood Comprehensive Plan future land use map. It actually has two classifications on this site. It calls it Greenwood Crossing and it calls for regional destination commercial land use. Let's look at what that means in your comprehensive plan. Regional destination commercial land use in your comprehensive plan says that this classification is designed to accommodate a range of potential entertainment, recreation, hospitality, and retail activities. There's no mention of residential activities in that opening paragraph describing regional destination commercial. That also goes on to say that those activities are generally in close proximity to Interstate 65. The site is right next to Interstate 65. It goes further on to say the defining characteristics of these uses is that customers will plan a special trip, there and value the overall experience. I think Buc-ee's meets a lot of those elements. So, you look down at the use table, it says the primary uses are retail, restaurant, recreation, entertainment, office, medical office, personal service, hotel, assisted living, event, venue center. Those are the kinds of uses you'd expect to develop around this Buc-ee’s and the kinds of uses that are allowed under this proposed planned unit of development. One thing that you also need to look at in the Comprehensive Plan that calls this Greenwood Crossing Conceptual Plan, it has some design principles. One of those design principles, the first one, is to develop a walkable mixed-use activity center serving as an anchor for new investment south of Worthsville. This is certainly new investment just south of Worthsville with a mix of commercial, hospitality, and office flex uses that capitalize on the interstate visibility. This site is right next to the interstate and access and have a potential to diversify the city's employment base, attract visitors, and fill the daily needs of nearby residents. We'll talk about that in a minute. But another element in that is city investment. It says the development should create a return on significant city investments in the area, including the sanitary sewer lift station, the sports park, extension of multi-use trails, and the fire station 95. This will represent a very significant investment. The zoning, underlying zoning, under the planet development zoning, is CL, commercial large zoning. And the plan commission has looked at this and also looked at the plat. The first thing to happen w

items.text: Meeting of the Greenwood Common Council ROLL CALL Date: October 5. 2026 Time: 7:00 pm Place: Council Chamber 300 S Madison Ave Greenwood, Indiana I. Call Meeting to Order A. Pledge of Allegiance B. Prayer: Gary Ryder, a long-time Greenwood resident and Air Traffic Controller C. Roll Call: Council Members Present: Mike Campbell ("Mr. Campbell"), Linda Gibson ("Ms. Gibson"), Ezra Hill ("Mr. Hill"), David Hopper ("Mr. Hopper"), Erin Kasch ("Ms. Kasch"), Teri Manship, ("Ms. Manship"), Steve Moan ("Mr. Moan") Darin Hoggatt ("Mr. Hoggatt") Absent: David Lekse, ("Mr. Lekse") City Officials: Mark Myers (“Mayor Myers”) Jeannine Myers ("Ms. Myers") Clerk, Greg Wright ("Mr. Wright") Controller, Sam Hodson (“Mr. Hodson”) Corporation Council, James Ison ("Chief Ison") Police Chief, Jayme Washel (“Chief Washel”) Fire Chief, and Department Heads. Council President Campbell reminded attendees that respectful participation is expected and that disruptions are not permitted. This will be read before each meeting: Before we begin, I want to remind everyone that respectful participation is expected. We welcome public input but there will be no yelling or interruptions that prevent the meeting from moving forward. Anyone who disrupts the meeting will be asked to leave and may be escorted out. II. Approval of Minutes A. Minutes from the regular meeting September 21,2026 Motion to postpone approval of minutes from September 9, 2026 by Moan, seconded by Manship. Votes: All Ayes B. Life Saving Award III. Reports A. Corporation Counsel B. Controller C. Committee & Board Report Greenwood Growth Speaker Series: TOPIC: What, Why, and Demand for Missing Middle Housing. Speaker(s): Chris Pryor, Chief Advocacy Officer, Brad Coffing, Director of Housing Insights IV. Public Comments This timeslot is for residents who would like to address the Council about matters on the agenda. All materials presented at a public meeting are considered part of the official record; please provide a copy to the Clerk. Individuals- 5-minute time limit; Groups- 20-minute time limit V. Ordinances and Resolutions A. Notice of Intent to Consider ORDINANCE NO. 26-36 AN ORDINANCE TO AMEND THE OFFICIAL ZONING MAP ADOPTED BY REFERENCE IN UNIFIED DEVELOPMENT ORDINANCE NO. 20-29 (PROPOSED REZONING OF APPROXIMATELY 48.21 ACRES OF LAND COMMONLY KNOWN AS 903 W. STONES CROSSING ROAD) (Sponsored by Lekse) Motion to amend Ord. No. 26-36 motion to remove the word “additional” from item #5 and add no vinyl by Hopper seconded by Hoggatt Votes: Ayes - Campbell, Gibson, Hill, Hoggatt, Hopper, Kasch, Manship, Hoggatt Votes: Nay-Moan Motion to pass Ord. No. 26-36 as amended by Hopper, seconded by Gibson Votes: Ayes - Gibson, Hill, Hoggatt, Hopper, Kasch, Manship, Moan, Campbell Motion passes: 8-0 B. First Reading ORDINANCE NO. 26-30 AN ORDINANCE FIXING THE SALARY OF THE COMMON COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF GREENWOOD, INDIANA FOR THE YEAR 2027 (Sponsored by Gibson, Kasch) Motion to pass Ord. No. 26-30 by Gibson, seconded by Kasch Votes: Ayes – Hill, Hoggatt, Hopper, Kasch, Manship, Moan, Campbell, Gibson Motion passes: 8-0 ORDINANCE NO. 26-31 AN ORDINANCE FIXING THE SALARY OF THE MAYOR OF THE CITY OF GREENWOOD, INDIANA FOR THE YEAR 2027 (Sponsored by Gibson, Kasch) Motion to pass Ord. No. 26-31 by Hoggatt, seconded by Manship Votes: Ayes – Hoggatt, Hopper, Kasch, Manship, Moan, Campbell, Gibson, Hill Motion passes: 8-0 ORDINANCE NO. 26-32 AN ORDINANCE FIXING THE SALARY OF THE CLERK OF THE CITY OF GREENWOOD, INDIANA FOR THE YEAR 2027 (Sponsored by Gibson, Kasch) Motion to pass Ord. No. 26-32 by Kasch, seconded by Moan Votes: Ayes -Hopper, Kasch, Manship, Moan, Campbell, Gibson, Hill, Hoggatt Motion passes: 8-0 ORDINANCE NO. 26-33 AN ORDINANCE FIXING THE SALARY OF THE CITY JUDGE OF THE CITY OF GREENWOOD, INDIANA FOR THE YEAR 2027(Sponsored by Gibson, Kasch) Motion to pass Ord. No. 26-09 by Hopper, seconded by Gibson Votes: Ayes - Gibson, Hill, Hoggatt, Hopper, Kasch, Manship, Moan, Campbell Motion passes: 8-0 Motion to pass Res. No. 26-09 second reading by Gibson, seconded by Moan Votes: Ayes - Hill, Hoggatt, Hopper, Kasch, Manship, Moan, Campbell, Gibson Motion passes: 8-0 C. Second Reading ORDINANCE NO. 26-29 AN ORDINANCE OF THE COMMON COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF GREENWOOD, INDIANA, AUTHORIZING AND ESTABLISHING THE BOUNDARIES OF FOUR MUNICIPAL RIVERFRONT DEVELOPMENT PROJECT AREAS WITHIN THE CITY OF GREENWOOD PURSUANT TO INDIANA CODE §7.1-3-20-16 AND INDIANA CODE §7.1-3-20-16.1 (Sponsored by Hill, Manship) Public Hearing Motion to pass Ord. No. 26-29 second reading by Kasch, seconded by Hoggatt Votes: Ayes –Hoggatt, Hopper, Kasch, Manship, Moan, Campbell, Gibson, Hill Motion passes: 8-0 D. New Business – Introductions of New Ordinances and Resolutions VII. Miscellaneous Business A. Public Comments This timeslot is for residents who would like to address the Council about matters not on the agenda. All materials presented at a public meeting are considered part of the official record; please provide a copy to the Clerk. Individuals- 5-minute time limit; Groups- 20-minute time limit. B. Council C. Other Miscellaneous A. Corporation Counsel B. Controller C. Mayor VIII. Adjournment In accordance with the American with Disabilities Act, the City of Greenwood is required to provide reasonable accommodations to persons with disabilities wishing to attend public meetings. Accommodations are available upon request to persons with disabilities who require alternately formatted materials, auxiliary aids, or reasonable modifications to policies and procedures to ensure effective communication and access to the public meeting. If you require accommodations to attend the meeting, please contact Public Access ADA Coordinator, Mr. Kevin Steinmetz at, 300 S. Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) provides resources to help Greenwood maintain decent housing, suitable living environments, and expand economic opportunity for low- and moderate-income citizens. Greenwood may only use CDBG to fund activities serving Greenwood residents.
Public Input Requested: Program Year 2026 Action Plan
Greenwood will receive $297,789 in Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) funding from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) for the 2026 Program Year (PY2026) running October 1, 2026 - September 30, 2027. The City invites residents, neighborhood groups, social service agencies, business community members, and interested citizens to participate in the development of the Action Plan.
CDBG Program Year 2026 Action Plan
How can you provide feedback?
1. Attend Public Hearing 2 on June 17, 2026, 6:30 PM
Greenwood Public Library, Community Room A, 310 South Meridian Street
Greenwood CDBG will present the projects, types of activities, and funding for the 2026 Program Year.
2. Provide a Public Comment June 18 - July 18, 2026
Greenwood will post the PY2026 Action Plan for review and public comments on this website and at the reference desk in the Greenwood Public Library. Commenters must include their name and ensure Greenwood receives comments by 5:00 PM on July 18, 2026. Greenwood will consider all formal public comments on the Action Plan before submitting the document and comments to HUD by August 14, 2026.
To submit a public comment, for further information, or to request an accommodation, please contact Kevin Steinmetz at cdbg@greenwood.in.gov , 317-887-5000 , or 300 South Madison Avenue, Greenwood, IN 46142. Please submit accommodation requests three business days in advance.

Mayor Myers Highlights Growth, Opportunities and Priorities at 2026 State of the City
Mayor Outlines City Achievements and Four Key Pillars that Guide Greenwood’s Future
Today, Greenwood Mayor Mark W. Myers delivered his fifteenth annual State of the City to more than 250 business professionals, community members and residents at the Greenwood Fieldhouse. Hosted by Aspire Economic Development + Chamber Alliance and moderated by Eric Prime of Van Valer Law Firm, the discussion centered on the city’s continued growth, its recent achievements and the priorities that will guide Greenwood through 2026 and beyond.
Mayor Myers framed the conversation around four pillars: public safety, infrastructure, quality of life and economic development – emphasizing how each plays a role in Greenwood’s continued success. While celebrating the city’s momentum, the Mayor also acknowledged challenges facing communities statewide, including the impacts of SEA 1, the recent property tax legislation.
“I’m excited about the growth and opportunities Greenwood has ahead in 2026,” said Mayor Myers. “Like any community, we may face challenges, but we are ready to meet them head on and continue building on the good work happening across our city. Greenwood’s success comes from the people who live, work and invest here.”
During the event, Mayor Myers highlighted major public safety investments, including expanded staffing within the Greenwood Fire Department and Greenwood Police Department, and continued training initiatives and progress on Fire Station 95, which will improve emergency response times and regional training opportunities.
Infrastructure remains a key focus, with Mayor Myers outlining recent road improvements, traffic enhancements and stormwater projects. He also discussed Greenwood’s continued use of state and federal funding, grants and partnerships to maximize the impact of infrastructure investments while planning responsibly for future needs.
The Mayor highlighted quality-of-life initiatives that continue to shape daily life in Greenwood, including parks programming, recreation amenities, community events and placemaking efforts. Greenwood’s recognition by U.S. News & World Report as one of the best places to live and retire reflects the city’s ongoing focus on a strong live, work and play balance.
Mayor Myers celebrated economic development successes, including 21 new businesses, continued job creation and investment throughout Greenwood. He also highlighted the first full year of operation at Greenwood Sports Park, which welcomed more than 70,000 visitors and generated over $218,000 in revenue.
The State of the City serves as an opportunity to recognize the work of city employees, partners and community members while outlining a clear vision for the year ahead.

Connect with Indiana 211 to Locate Local Warming Centers This Winter
During the winter weather season, warming centers are available across Indiana to provide a safe, warm place for individuals in need. Indiana 211 offers the most up-to-date information on warming center locations and hours in your community.
Call: Speak directly with a Community Navigator. Phone: Dial 2-1-1 or 1-866-211-9966 Available Monday - Friday, 8 a.m. to 6 p.m.
Text: Get a list of warming centers near you. Text your ZIP Code to 898-211 Available Monday - Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.
Online Search: Find warming centers through the Indiana 211 resource database at IN211.org .
To report a new warming center or update an existing listing, contact Indiana 211’s resource team by email at in211database@fssa.in.gov .

A través de la innovación, la colaboración y un profundo compromiso con la excelencia, este plan transformará las Escuelas de la Ciudad de Beech Grove, asegurando que nuestros estudiantes, personal y familias se sientan conectados, apoyados y preparados para el éxito de por vida. Estamos profundamente agradecidos por las voces, ideas y compromisos que han dado forma a este plan. Juntos, no solo estamos imaginando un futuro más brillante, sino que lo estamos construyendo activamente, asegurando que cada estudiante tenga la confianza, las oportunidades y el apoyo para prosperar. El trabajo que tenemos por delante es transformador, y nos sentimos honrados de embarcarnos en este viaje con nuestra comunidad. Con gratitud y determinación, Es con gran orgullo que compartimos el Plan Estratégico de las Escuelas de la Ciudad de Beech Grove, una hoja de ruta para nuestros estudiantes, personal y comunidad. Este plan refleja las voces de casi 2,000 partes interesadas que participaron en encuestas y grupos focales, junto con la dedicación de nuestro Comité Directivo, que incluyó a maestros, líderes, padres y miembros de la comunidad. Trabajando juntos, podemos afirmar con confianza que este plan se alinea con los valores y aspiraciones de Beech Grove. items.title: Download the Plan (English)
items.text: Beech Grove City SchoolsStrategic Plan 2025 Community Engagement and Communication – Strengthening partnerships and ensuring every voice is heard Wellness and Belonging – Creating safe and welcoming spaces where all students, families, and staff feel valued and supported Teaching and Learning – Delivering engaging, high-quality educational opportunities that ensure all students have the support and access they need to succeed Leadership Development – Investing in our educators and staff to grow strong leaders at every level. Through innovation, collaboration, and a deep commitment to excellence, this plan will transform Beech Grove City Schools—ensuring that our students, staff, and families feel connected, supported, and prepared for lifelong success. We are deeply grateful for the voices, ideas, and commitments that have shaped this plan. Together, we are not just envisioning a brighter future—we are actively building it, ensuring that every student has the confidence, opportunities, and support to thrive. The work ahead is transformative, and we are honored to embark on this journey with our community. With gratitude and determination, It is with great pride that we share the Beech Grove City Schools Strategic Plan, a roadmap for our students, staff, and community. This plan reflects the voices of nearly 2,000 stakeholders who participated in surveys and focus groups, along with the dedication of our Steering Committee, which included teachers, leaders, parents, and community members. Working together, we can confidently assert that this plan aligns with the values and aspirations of Beech Grove. At the heart of this plan is our fierce commitment to student success, guided by our vision, mission, core values, and beliefs. We envision Beech Grove City Schools to be a place where all students believe that education is the way to change the world, and through this plan, we will ensure every student in Beech Grove has the opportunities, support, and experiences needed to thrive. Our strategic goals are centered around four key areas: Dear Hornet Family, Dr. Laura Hammack, Superintendent of Beech Grove City Schools 5 Schools. 1 Family.In our schools, you’ll hear us talk about family and being stronger and better together. We are known for putting ‘we before me.’ Words matter and we use them with care. #Together #WeBeforeMe Vision Mission Beech Grove City Schools – where all students believe education is the way to change their world. We hold high expectations for every student by: 1) Delivering highly engaging educational opportunities 2) Designing individualized access, and 3) Developing student ownership for learning so every student is positioned for success the day they walk across the stage at graduation Values CommunityBelonging We create safe spaces where everyone feels welcomed, connected and valued. We place others above ourselves by serving and partnering with our community. We recognize and celebrate that our differences make us stronger

beech grove common council
The Beech Grove Common Council is comprised of seven members elected to four-year terms; two at-large and five elected from the five Council districts. The Council is the legislative body of the city. It adopts the annual budget for the city, appropriates tax monies, passes city ordinances and resolutions, and makes appointments to certain boards and commissions. Regular meetings of the Com mon Council are held at 7:00 p.m. on the first Monday of each month. In the event the regular meeting day falls on a legal holiday, the meeting will be held the day following the holiday. Special meetings may called by the Mayor with at least three days notice and for a specified purpose. The Mayor, or in his or her absence the President Pro-Tempore of the Common Council, serves as presiding officer. Email the entire council at citycouncil@beechgrove.com .

New plumbing apprenticeship training center to officially open in Beech Grove, transforming longtimevacant site in the heart of the city
(Beech Grove, Ind.) Mechanical Skills, Inc. and the City of Beech Grove will celebrate the grand opening of a new plumbing apprenticeship training center on Monday, Aug. 10 , marking the completion of a project that has transformed a longtime vacant parcel into a hub for the skilled trades in the heart of the city.
Located at 1831 Albany Street, the site was once home to a Marsh and Safeway grocery store before sitting vacant for years. The new 20,000-square-foot facility now serves as a center for education and workforce development, while bringing new investment and activity to a key corridor adjacent to Main Street.

items.title: Code of Conduct
items.text: PERRY TOWNSHIP ATHLETIC CODE OF CONDUCT A. Preface The Perry Township Athletic Code of Conduct does not supersede the Student Rights & Responsibilities Policy for Students, Parents, and School Personnel of Perry Township Schools. Individuals may receive discipline under both discipline codes. It is the belief of the coaches, administrators, and school board of Perry Township that participation in athletics is a privilege, not a right, and that as a representative of the school, school system, and community, the athlete is expected to assume certain responsibilities and to live up to certain expectations. It is the purpose of this document to clarify those expectations. A coach may have additional written team rules not addressed in this code. Situations not addressed in this code will be addressed by the building principal. B. The Responsibilities of a Perry Township Athlete: A student/athlete is expected to: 1. Achieve academically to the best of the student’s abilities. Each student’s first responsibility is to be a good student. 2. Act in accordance with high standards of social behavior. 3. Display good sportsmanship both on and off the field. 4. Show respect to opponents, teammates, officials, spectators, coaches, and administrators. 5. Maintain a good appearance including dress, grooming, and cleanliness. 6. Use language that reflects positively on school, community, and family. This includes information shared on social media sites. 7. Be a positive leader in the classroom, on the playing field, in the school, and in the community. 8. Comply with these guidelines in and out of season, on and off the playing field, at school and away from school. C. Eligibility: High School 1. In order to be eligible according to the IHSAA, a student athlete must: a. Have a completed physical form/release form on file with the athletic director of the student’s respective school. b. Have passed five (5) or more full credit subjects during the past grading period and currently enrolled in five (5) or more full credit subjects. 2. If an athlete quits a team while in-season, that athlete is ineligible to participate in another sport unless released by the Athletic Director. This includes pre-season workouts. 31 D. Eligibility: Academy/Middle School (nine-week grade requirements and other eligibility standards) 1. Students in the 6th, 7th, and 8th grade can fail no more than one subject. 2. Students can meet the requirements using either the last nine-week grades of the second semester or the yearly final grades to be eligible for the fall season. 3. A student who is ineligible for the fall season will be permitted to try out for a winter sport provided the student’s grades indicate that the student will be eligible at the end of the first nine-weeks grading period. 4. By Emily Steinmetz | Jul 31, 2026 9:29 AM
Perry Meridian Athletics Earns State and National Recognition for Excellence Perry Meridian High School Athletics is proud to announce that our athletic department has received two of the highest recognitions available at the state and national levels, affirming our commitment to providing an outstanding education-based athletic experience for every Falcon. For the 2025-2026 school year, Perry Meridian Athletics has been recognized as an IHSAA Sportsmanship Banner School and has also earned the National Interscholastic Athletic Administrators Association (NIAAA) Quality Program Recognition at the Exemplary Level. While championships and victories are celebrated, these honors recognize something even more meaningful—the daily work of building a culture where student-athletes grow as leaders, teammates, and people of character. IHSAA Sportsmanship Banner The Indiana High School Athletic Association (IHSAA) awarded Perry Meridian Athletics its 2025-2026 Sportsmanship Banner, recognizing schools that intentionally promote positive sportsmanship, leadership, and respect throughout their athletic programs. To earn this distinction, schools must demonstrate excellence in four key areas: Outstanding sportsmanship throughout the school year -Student-athlete leadership development -Meaningful community outreach -Intentional efforts to create a positive school culture This recognition reflects the actions of our student-athletes, coaches, parents, administrators, officials, and fans who consistently represent Perry Meridian with integrity and class. National Exemplary Recognition Perry Meridian Athletics has also been selected by the National Interscholastic Athletic Administrators Association (NIAAA) to receive the 2026 Quality Program Recognition at the Exemplary Level—one of the highest honors awarded to high school athletic programs nationwide. The Quality Program Assessment is a comprehensive evaluation of an athletic department's philosophy, leadership, operations, risk management, educational practices, communication, and commitment to continuous improvement. Schools earning the Exemplary distinction provide extensive evidence that their policies, procedures, and daily practices meet the highest professional standards established by the NIAAA. As part of this recognition, Perry Meridian Athletics will be honored during a national ceremony in December, recognized at the 2026 NIAAA National Conference in Phoenix, Arizona, and featured in national publications highlighting exemplary athletic programs across the country. items.title: IHSAA Myths
items.text: IHSAA Myths Let’s debunk the TOP 9 most common Myths and misconceptions about the IHSAA: #1 Myth: The IHSAA is funded by taxpayer dollars. FACT: The IHSAA is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization. We do not receive government funding. Revenue is derived from tournament ticket sales, corporate partnerships, media rights fees, and licensing contest officials. #2 Myth: The IHSAA is a large government organization. FACT: The IHSAA is a small private educational nonprofit with a large impact— overseeing and organizing education-based athletics for 409 voluntary member high schools across all 92 Indiana counties. Our 20 staff members are responsible for administering state tournaments, licensing contest officials, and enforcing our membership’s bylaws in order to maintain fair and equitable learning opportunities in education-based athletics. #3 Myth: The IHSAA Commissioner and Assistant Commissioners create all IHSAA rules. FACT: IHSAA bylaws are created by and voted on by our member schools and their elected representatives(board of directors). All IHSAA staff are hired by those same elected representatives to provide services to our 409 member schools, which includes enforcing our membership’s bylaws and rules. #4 Myth: The IHSAA can change rules at any point and has flexibility in applying rules. FACT: IHSAA rules can only be enacted or changed by a majority vote of the IHSAA board of directors who are elected by the IHSAA member schools they represent. IHSAA staff are bound to apply those rules as written. When our membership wants to change a rule, an appeals process is in place. #5 Myth: The IHSAA realigns Sectionals for team class sports at random. FACT: IHSAA committees audit and scrutinize Sectional alignment every two years, taking many factors into consideration for the entire state rather than any singular area. Committees are made up of superintendents, principals, and athletic directors representing different regions and school sizes around the state. #6 Myth: The IHSAA profits from high school athletics. FACT: Annually, the IHSAA distributes more money back to our membership (over $2.8 million in 2023-24) than we retain for operating costs. For instance, we return 98% of Sectional ticket revenue from our most profitable sports back to our member schools. #7 Myth: The IHSAA always denies athletic eligibility for transfer students. FACT: Annually, 99% of transfer students are granted a path to athletic eligibility. Of our ~160,000 student-athletes, ~4,000 transfer schools (2.5%), and fewer than 50 of those student- athletes are not granted eligibility (1.2% of 2.5%). We always approach transfer cases with the mindset of helping student-athletes find a path to participation, but when eligibility is denied, that decision is made to protect the opportunities of every student-athlete impacted by a transfer. #8 Myth: The IHSAA just runs tournaments that determine the best athletes and teams in the state. FACT: Crowning state champions may be what
